value.text:
Linemen do not win trophies. Jakeem Friend won six rings instead.

For most of his career he was a Seattle Seahawk, a fixture up front through the Modern era. He has played 232 games and been credited with 482 blocks, two a game, every game, without a single MVP or Player of the Year award to show for it. That is how the job works. The reward is a quarterback who gets up clean and a running back who finds the hole where it was supposed to be.

The last three seasons have come in New York, with the Jets from Y79 to Y81. The jersey changed. The job did not, and Seattle still has first claim on him.

Six rings, 482 blocks, and almost no headlines. Jakeem Friend, Seahawks legend, welcome to the Hall of Fame.

value.text:
One look at Scary Jerry and you understood the name.

Jason Macleone was imposing before he ever threw a pass, and then he threw 9,462 of them. He completed 67 percent for 70,010 yards and 733 touchdowns, with just 126 interceptions across 313 games. He took 85 sacks and never lost a fumble. When he did tuck it and run, he made it count: 67 rushing touchdowns.

His defining day came in Y78, when he quarterbacked the Vikings past the Broncos 33-27 in Super Bowl CXXXVII. Two rings, three MVPs and a Super Bowl MVP in all, and he is still slinging it in Seattle, where every new start adds to the case.

The league's line of great quarterbacks runs from Lamar through Gooden, Waller, Baylon, Brandson and the Wilson brothers. For now, it ends with him. Scary Jerry, welcome to the Hall of Fame.

value.text:
The best offensive lineman in the league never needed a highlight. He just needed a man in front of him.

Cooper Dean anchored the Commanders' line for 292 games and recorded 345 blocks, nearly three hundred games of the least glamorous work in football. Every clean pocket and every open running lane started with somebody like him, and for most of his career there was nobody quite like him. Quarterbacks stayed upright. Running backs found daylight. The man responsible rarely heard his name over the stadium speakers.

He was called the best lineman in the league, and nobody put up much of an argument. His one ring came in Y19, the last title of the Commanders' four-peat under the coach who built this league's dynasties. After the coach moved on, Dean spent the rest of his career trying to hold those dynasties back. That ring was the reward for doing the job right on every snap.

Linemen do not usually get the last word. Cooper Dean, welcome to the Hall of Fame.

value.text:
He changed his name to God. Then he earned it.

Mason Earl III walked into the league as a receiver. God Johnson walked out as the standard every receiver gets measured against. Some people thought the name was a joke. Defensive coordinators never laughed.

36,005 receiving yards. 378 receiving touchdowns. Ten rings, from Miami to the Vikings dynasty, and five Super Bowl MVPs, because when the lights were brightest the ball found him. And three fumbles. In his entire career. Ian Finney's career receiving mark stood for decades until God took it, with Jackson Wardell Kline lined up beside him.

There is not much left to say about a man who named himself after the only being with a better résumé. God Johnson, welcome to the Hall of Fame.

value.text:
2,658 tackles from a defensive back. Read that again.

Dan Mosley played in the secondary like a linebacker who had wandered back to cover. Over 248 games he averaged more than ten tackles a game, a number most run stoppers never touch. And he still found the ball in the air, with 37 career interceptions. A hitter and a ballhawk in the same Lions jersey.

He did it in the Modern era, a decade of three-peats and title runs. Detroit was never the team lifting the trophy, and Mosley arrives without a ring. What he does have is a Defensive Player of the Year award, the most heavily weighted honor in this league's Dominance formula, worth twice as much as a ring.

Nobody had to tell ball carriers where Dan Mosley was. They found out. Dan Mosley, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
